query: For high-entropy alloys intended for demanding engineering applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs the retention or loss of toughness, and why? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, the predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In single‐phase fcc high‐entropy alloys, toughness is retained when grain boundary cohesion is maintained, but toughness is lost when principal elements (e.g., Cr, Ni, and Mn) rapidly nanocluster at grain boundaries and thereby reduce interfacial cohesion. By engineering the grain boundaries—for example, by inducing pre‐existing Cr-rich secondary phases that redirect or suppress the deleterious nanoclustering—the alloy can retain its toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: A polycrystalline, single‐phase face‐centered cubic high‐entropy alloy (e.g., CrMnFeCoNi) with a uniform chemical distribution in the grain interiors and naturally susceptible to nanosegregation at grain boundaries under deformation.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled heat treatment designed to promote the formation of pre‐existing Cr-rich secondary phases at or near grain boundaries. This treatment is intended to provide alternative sinks for the fast-segregating elements, thereby reducing their accumulation (nanoclustering) along the grain boundaries.
generation.conditions: The alloy is deformed (e.g., via tensile testing) under intermediate temperature conditions where diffusion is active but does not cause extensive phase transformation. The comparison is made between the baseline (no heat treatment) and the treated alloy under identical strain rate and temperature conditions to assess changes in fracture toughness and ductility.
generation.structural_mediator: The chemical state and cohesion of the grain boundaries mediated by the distribution (or nanoclustering) of principal elements (especially Cr, Ni, and Mn).
generation.mechanism: Rapid nanosegregation of certain principal elements at grain boundaries reduces localized cohesion, promoting intergranular cracking and thus lowering total toughness. Conversely, if a controlled heat treatment pre-distributes these elements into Cr-rich secondary phases, the harmful segregation at the grain boundaries is suppressed, maintaining stronger, more ductile intergranular interfaces.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline alloy, the treated alloy with engineered grain boundaries will exhibit higher fracture toughness and improved ductility. In microstructural characterization (e.g., via atom probe tomography), there should be reduced nanoclustering at grain boundaries in the treated sample compared to the untreated state.
generation.baseline: The as-cast (or as-processed) single-phase CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy exhibiting naturally developing nanoclusters at the grain boundaries during deformation, which leads to premature intergranular fracture.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold for polycrystalline, single-phase fcc high-entropy alloys in the intermediate temperature regime (where atomic diffusion is moderately active) and for alloys with similar principal-element chemistries (e.g., CrMnFeCoNi).
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of toughness improvement and the optimal heat-treatment conditions (temperature, time) to produce the desired Cr-rich secondary phases are not fully defined. Additionally, the temperature window over which grain-boundary nanosegregation governs toughness remains to be precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of the same CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy samples. The control group remains in the as-processed state, while the experimental group is subjected to a specific heat treatment aimed at forming Cr-rich secondary phases at the grain boundaries. Characterize both groups using atom probe tomography and high-resolution TEM to assess grain boundary chemistry and nanoclustering. Then perform tensile tests at an intermediate temperature and a constant strain rate to measure fracture toughness and ductility.
measurements: Fracture toughness (e.g., via notch toughness or tensile tests)
Grain boundary chemistry and nanoclustering profiles (via APT/TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the engineered (heat-treated) alloy does not show a statistically significant increase in fracture toughness/delayed intergranular fracture compared to the baseline, or if microstructural analysis reveals that the heat treatment did not substantially reduce the extent of harmful nanoclustering at the grain boundaries, then the hypothesis that grain boundary nanosegregation governs toughness retention/loss would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Nanoclustering Cr, Ni, and Mn separately at GBs reduces GB cohesion in single-phase CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloys. AbstractThe loss of ductility with temperature has been widely observed in tensile tests of single-phase face-centered cubic structured high-entropy alloys (HEAs). However, the fundamental mechanism for such a ductility loss remains unknown. Here, we show that ductility loss in the CrMnFeCoNi HEA upon deformation at intermediate temperatures is correlated with cracking at grain boundaries (GBs). Nanoclustering Cr, Ni, and Mn separately at GBs, as detected by atom probe tomography, reduces GB cohesion and promotes crack initiation along GBs. We further demonstrated a GB segregation engineering strategy to avoid ductility loss by shifting the fast segregation of principal elements from GBs into preexisting Cr-rich secondary phases. We believe that GB decohesion by nanoclustering multiprincipal elements is a common phenomenon in HEAs. This study not only provides insights into understanding ductility loss but also offers a strategy for tailoring ductility-temperature relations in HEAs.

We revealed the key mechanism responsible for the loss of the ductility with increasing temperature, a phenomenon widely reported in the single-phase fcc HEAs that are composed of three or more elements of Al, Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, and Ni. SEM of tensioned sample surfaces of single-phase coarse-grained Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 HEA (grain size around 50 μm) suggested that ductility loss is correlated with the intergranular cracking. However, TEM along GBs confirmed that there are no precipitates of secondary phases along GBs. On the basis of APT analysis, we explored that ductility loss is attributed to fast nanosegregation of principal elements Ni, Cr, and Mn separately into GBs, which reduce GB cohesion and promote crack initiation along GBs. We further demonstrated a GB segregation engineering strategy to evade ductility loss by migrating fast segregation of the principal elements from GBs into preexisting Cr-rich secondary phases in an example HEA, i.e., Cr26Mn20Fe20Co20Ni14. Our work not only provides insights into understanding ductility loss but also offers a GB segregation engineering strategy of tailoring strength-ductility-temperature relations in HEAs.
